To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) there is a clear offset of the fundamental plane at z ≃ 0.4 between field and cluster samples; (2) this offset is in the direction expected from accelerated evolution in dense environments; (3) the offset is independent of mass; and (4) it cannot be explained by a mass-dependent downsizing effect.

the fundamental plane of galactic bulge properties is environmentally dependent at fixed redshift, and that this dependence cannot be explained by the mass-dependent downsizings effects seen in larger galaxy samples.

In summary, our research is concerned with
environmental effects on the evolution of galaxies, and in particular, the evolution of the bulge component.
the evolution of galaxies and their constituent components in dense environments.
the evolution of bulges within the framework of hierarchical galaxy formation and the role of environmental factors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the observed environmental dependence is not a result of the downsizing effects, and it is not consistent with the idea of a purely secular evolution for the bulges.
the observed trends in the FP are consistent with a combination of downsizing effects, which are mass-dependent, and environmental effects, which are independent of mass.
the environmental dependence of the zero point of the fundamental plane for bulges at z ∼ 0.5 is consistent with the picture of accelerated evolution in dense environments.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the environmental trends in the FP of galactic bulge components are consistent with the idea that the evolution of these components is driven primarily by star formation and that the evolution of the star formation rate is environmentally dependent.

the environmental dependence of the FP zero point for galaxies at 0.4 < z < 1.0 is a robust result, and that this trend can be explained by accelerated evolution of the bulge component in dense environments.
the evolution of galaxy bulges is not independent of environment and that this evolution is accelerated in dense environments. © 2008.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the environment plays a significant role in the evolution of bulges, with the most massive galaxies in dense environments evolving faster and more efficiently than their counterparts in low-density regions.

environmental effects play an important role in shaping the properties of bulges, and that these effects may be more significant than those associated with the mass-dependent star formation history of galaxies.
, at fixed stellar mass, the environmental dependence of bulge evolution is significant and cannot be neglected in future studies of bulge formation and evolution.
